lessons.title: Fractions
lessons.summary: A fraction names equal parts of a whole and helps us compare and combine parts.

sections.heading: Equal parts
sections.passage: A fraction describes equal parts of one whole. The denominator is the number below the line and tells how many equal parts make the whole. The numerator is the number above the line and tells how many of those parts we choose. For example, 3/4 means three of four equal parts.

sections.heading: Comparing fractions
sections.passage: When two fractions have the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is greater. When denominators are different, find a common denominator. The fractions 1/2 and 2/4 name the same amount because 2/4 can be simplified to 1/2.

sections.heading: Fractions in daily life
sections.passage: We use fractions when sharing food, measuring ingredients and reading time. Half a roti, one quarter of a chapati and three quarters of a glass are everyday fractions. A fraction can also be shown on a number line between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: What does the denominator tell us?
choices: How many equal parts make the whole
questions.answer: How many equal parts make the whole
questions.explanation: The denominator is below the fraction line and names the number of equal parts in the whole.

questions.prompt: In the fraction 3/4, what does 3 show?
questions.explanation: The numerator counts the chosen parts, so 3 of the 4 equal parts are chosen.
With the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is greater.
2/4 simplifies to 1/2 because both numbers can be divided by 2.

questions.prompt: A roti is cut into 4 equal parts. You eat 1 part. What fraction did you eat?
questions.explanation: One chosen part out of four equal parts is written as 1/4.

lessons.title: Decimals
lessons.summary: Decimals write fractions of tenths and hundredths using a decimal point.

sections.heading: Tenths and hundredths
sections.passage: The first digit after the decimal point shows tenths. The second digit shows hundredths. The decimal 0.3 means three tenths, or 3/10. The decimal 0.35 means thirty-five hundredths, or 35/100. The decimal point separates whole numbers from parts of a whole.

sections.heading: Comparing decimals
sections.passage: Compare digits from left to right. Start with the whole numbers, then tenths, then hundredths. The decimal 0.7 is greater than 0.65 because seven tenths is more than six tenths. Adding a zero after the last decimal digit does not change the value, so 0.5 is equal to 0.50.

sections.heading: Money and measurement
sections.passage: Rupees and paise use decimals: 12.50 rupees means twelve rupees and fifty paise. Lengths such as 1.5 metres mean one metre and five tenths of a metre. Decimals help us read and compare measurements quickly.

questions.explanation: The first digit after the decimal point shows tenths, so 0.3 is 3/10.
Seven tenths is more than six tenths, so 0.7 is greater.
A zero after the last decimal digit does not change the value.
The digits after the decimal point show paise in a money amount.

questions.prompt: In 0.35, the digit 5 is in which place?
questions.explanation: The second digit after the decimal point is the hundredths place.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis
lessons.summary: Plants make food using light, water and carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: What plants need
sections.passage: Green plants make their own food. They need sunlight, water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air. The green substance chlorophyll in leaves captures light energy.

sections.heading: What plants produce
sections.passage: Photosynthesis makes sugar, called glucose, which the plant uses for energy and growth. Oxygen is released into the air as a by-product. This is one reason plants are important for the air we breathe.

sections.heading: Leaves and light
sections.passage: Leaves are shaped and arranged to catch sunlight. Tiny openings called stomata let carbon dioxide enter and oxygen leave. Water travels from the roots through the stem to the leaves.

questions.prompt: Which gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Plants take carbon dioxide from the air through tiny openings in the leaves.
Chlorophyll is the green substance that captures light energy in leaves.

questions.prompt: Which gas is released by photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released into the air as a by-product of photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Where does the water needed by a plant come from?
questions.explanation: Water is taken from the soil by the roots and travels up the stem.
Photosynthesis produces glucose, a sugar the plant uses for energy and growth.

lessons.title: Components of Food
lessons.summary: Food gives us energy and the materials our bodies need to grow, repair and stay healthy.

sections.heading: Nutrients
sections.passage: Carbohydrates and fats give energy. Proteins help the body grow and repair itself. Vitamins and minerals protect us from disease and keep our body working well. Water is also needed for digestion and for carrying nutrients.

sections.heading: A balanced diet
sections.passage: A balanced diet includes energy-giving foods, body-building foods and protective foods in the right amounts. Dal, rice, vegetables, fruit, milk and eggs are examples. No single food contains everything we need.

sections.heading: Food and health
sections.passage: Too little food can make a person weak. Too much oily or sugary food can cause health problems. Washing food and hands helps prevent illness. A varied diet and clean water support good health.

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates and fats are energy-giving nutrients.
Proteins are body-building nutrients used for growth and repair.
A balanced diet combines different kinds of food in the right amounts.

questions.prompt: Which choice is a protective food?
questions.explanation: Fruit and vegetables provide vitamins and minerals that protect us from disease.

questions.prompt: Why should we wash our hands before eating?
questions.explanation: Clean hands reduce the chance of germs getting into our food.
